I knew that the cast and I were on the same page about the psychology of the characters, because we did a lot of ground work in exploring the psychology of the characters. I therefore trusted them in performance. However, you still have to guide because the director is the only person on set who sees the big picture before it is a concrete thing that exists in an objective sense. I have to be sure that everyone’s instincts are working towards the eventual big picture. Same with the brilliant cinematographer Narayan Van Maele, Zjena Glamocanin on costume, Nicola Moroney on art dept. They are all marvellously talented people, but I have to be sure that all the disparate threads of their work are going to tie into the same ‘rope’ at the end of the day. In post-production, of course, there is more opportunity to try things out and it is great pleasure to work with a great editor (in this case, the magician who is John Murphy) and composer (the utterly magnificent Die Hexen) and push each other as far as we can go creatively, but it does always come back to ‘what is this film saying? What is the central thesis of it?’ and that has to come from me. That is really what the director’s job is. It simply can’t be done well in a collaboration that is in any way democratic. I think there’s a narrative when it comes to female directors that democratic collaboration is our principle mode of working, because we are expected to be nice and to be egoless, when in reality that would likely lead to a very messy and unfocused film, but it would also mean there is very little need for a director at all. It’s a way of removing some of the perceived status of director from women and casting us in a more socially acceptable role where we are nice ladies who are organising things, as if a film set could function like a church fundraiser. I am not the classic idea of the male director barking orders and insults through a loudspeaker, but I am also not a facilitator or helpmeet of some kind. I deeply respect the creatives and the skilled work people I have been privileged to work with, but I make films to express my observations about the world - which is, I think, why art is made generally. What would the purpose be otherwise? Everything must ultimately be filtered through that clarity of vision. I don’t think any of the above named creatives would want it to be any other way, no matter which director they are working with.

Questions after seeing the film
1) A big theme I took from the film was intergenerational trauma and the cycle it perpetuates. Was this theme something that was involved in the initial first draft of the script, or is this a theme that grew with the story?

To expand a little on the first question: the theme of intergenerational trauma - which is to me the most Irish of Irish cultural traits - was there from an early stage as an abstract idea, but it really became solidified in the characters as I was writing them. As they became who they were, it became obvious how their experiences needed to intersect and how they would thematically resonate with each other.

2) There is a lot of religious symbolism, both pagan and catholic, throughout and I guess this echoes my earlier question of did the religious aspect feel very important to this story in particular?

Any film that is about irishness, or where we are culturally as a people (albeit my subjective lens on that) would have to incorporate religious symbolism. As I’ve already said, Irish Catholicism has its own texture and that texture is folksy and a bit pagan. For me folk horror in Ireland is inextricable from religious horror. The two go hand in hand whereas elsewhere they are almost polar opposites. I knew early on that the villagers would dismiss Peig’s claim that she spent time in the Other World with Na Sídhe as a fantasy to protect her from a truth about being in a Magdalene Laundry or a Mother and Baby Home or something similar, because that is exactly how contemporary Irish people would interpret this. We know in our bones that the Catholic Church state and the dark hidden world of Na Sídhe are mirrors of each other. This is why the Na Sídhe are so bureaucratic too. They are a mirror of the Irish state which, at its founding, went directly from gun toting rebellion to constitutionally writing Irish women back into the kitchen. I think it’s interesting that the Na Sídhe of Irish folklore, with their multitude of arbitrary rules about what you can and can’t do, and the new Irish church state both relied on bureaucracy to control and subjugate the population.

3)3) I really loved the relation of Irish History to horror, and when listed like that really highlights the true horror of that history. Did you find yourself pulling a lot from that history to tell this story?

I don’t think that Ireland has truly reckoned with the effects of our troubled history on the collective psyche. So one doesn’t really have to draw on that history specifically to tell the story, that history is there in the background whether we like it or not. People still alive now lived in the society that turned blind eyes to Magdelene laundries, Mother and Baby homes, borstals, and industrial schools. People still alive were affected in different ways by the church’s sexual abuse scandals. Many people still living were directly affected by the Troubles. There are people still living who underwent symphisotemies and as a result they suffer with lifelong disabilities, to pick one example from many examples of historical Irish suffering that is not as historical as we wish it was. We are all close to the horrific effects of these things, the mental health issues that have resulted from these things, the neighbouring dominoes of addiction, alcoholism, self-harm and suicide rates, so the story doesn’t have to make any of them explicit - they all feed into the horror and anxiety that is central to the story and a big part of being Irish.

Closing Thoughts

A truly great experience at BFF for the second year in a row. They honestly outdid themselves; I enjoyed last year so much I did not think this year could be any better, and I was wonderfully proved wrong. The moment this year’s festival wrapped, I could already feel the excitement building up for next year. See you in 2025 BFF!
